#3760. The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time’s First Few Hours Are Stuffed With Overwhelming Extravagance

Nintendo Switch 2The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

Wow! The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is beautiful, yes, certainly the loveliest game Nintendo has ever made. The details, the colors, the sounds, the constant movements of individual leaves in light breezes, the ripple of water…wow! It’s dazzling! The stitching on Link’s tunic. All the unique bits of foliage that rustle as you walk through, the way nothing seems to obviously clip into anything else. The gentle reactions when you bump into NPCs. The attention to detail, everywhere, in the characters, the pacing, the way dungeon mechanisms work, everywhere you look, so much.

One of the Kokiri has a line at some point about how they and the fairies all sparkle and shine, and these visuals have committed to that descriptor. I didn’t want to leave the forest. But also I really, really did, especially after a little over an hour playing last night. Because it almost feels extravagant, like a just slightly uncomfortable excess, especially after having played the sparse original so recently. This new visual density fills in gaps where the imagination used to do the work. I stop more than short of shaking my fist at this, decrying kids these days for having no creativity. I think the abundance of Kokiri Forest, rendered this way, is wonderful, but it also leaves me with a wistfulness for something a bit less much.Â I don’t know where the line of “exactly the right amount of everything” is, and I certainly think toeing it would be a worse decision than this. I just can’t help but feel a bit unnerved by it.

And the dialogue! At first, my gut reaction is that everyone talks too damn much. The game’s introduction felt interminable. Saria strikes me as corny and tedious. Why? I sat down and compared the dialogue from the original to this, and most of it isn’t much longer in the new version. Some of it is even basically the same. So what’s the difference?

Is it the presence of voice acting? Maybe. I love a good voice performance, but I have historically struggled with remakes that add voices where previously there were none. You’ll never stop hearing the characters as they were originally heard in your head, and the “real” voices will never feel right. But more regrettably, adding fully voiced cutscenes means that Nintendo felt compelled to make sure every character got to participate. Especially Navi. No matter how useless it is to the conversation that she speak.

Here, compare. This is the dialogue of the Deku Tree to Navi in the original game, before sending her to get Link. Navi does not say a word until after she leaves:

Navi…Navi, where art thou? Come hither…Oh, Navi the fairy…listen to my words, the words of the Deku Tree. Dost thou sense it? The climate of evil descending upon this realm…Malevolent forces even now are mustering to attack our land of Hyrule,….For so long, the Kokiri Forest, the source of life, has stood as a barrier, deterring outsiders and maintaining the order of the world. But…before this tremendous evil power, even my power is as nothing. It seems the time has come for the boy without a fairy to begin his journey…The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the path of justice and truth. Navi…go now! Find our young friend and guide him to me…I do not have much time left. Fly, Navi, fly! The fate of the forest, nay, the world, depends upon thee!

Here’s the comparable version in the new game.

Deku Tree: It would seem…I have but a little time left…My heart feels heavy. Soon I will no longer be able to protect the forest. I must ensure its safety. I will entrust everything to the child. Navi…Little Navi, where are you?

Navi: Yes, Great Deku Tree. I’m here! How can I be of service?

Deku Tree: Ah, there you are. I have something to ask of you. I hope it is not too much. There is someone with whom I must speak. bring this young one to me.

Deku Tree: The only child in the forest without a fairy companion. His name is Link.

The first version is certainly fantastical. No one talks like that, with thees and thous and such, and it’s very much video game writing of its time in its unnecessary grandiosity. I won’t pretend that’s high literature or anything. But I hate the new stuff more, which comes off like an overwrought children’s play. I feel the same way about the Deku Tree’s later lines to Link (with Navi’s interjections), all the conversations with Saria, and Kaepora Gaebora’s truncated greeting of Link at the entrance of Hyrule Field. Pretty much any major story cutscene I’ve seen so far has felt off to me like this, full of unnecessary detail and oddly stilted ways of speaking.

The NPC dialogue in between all this is, of course, far better, and thank God for that, because I love Ocarina‘s cast of weird freaks. It helps that most of their lines audibly sound the way they did in the original, even if the words have been tweaked, because they get some sort of vocal exclamation (“Ah!” “Oh!” “Ohhhhh?” “Aha!” etc.) and then written text for you to fill in as you like mentally alongside appropriately over-the-top animations. Mido remains a delightful loser, road signs are still rife with great jokes, and the developers somehow managed to improve the beggar who desperately and with wild gesticulations pleads for you to sell him something. There are even some new guys, like the beard guy in Castle Town, who I feel would have fit right in in the original game even if he’s very clearly like Guy #10 in a lineup of NPCs intended to encourage Link to follow the story and go to the castle, just in case you hadn’t figured out that’s where you were supposed to go yet.

I also can’t fully knock the effect that a more detailed game has on the gravitas of Ocarina of Time‘s story. After you’re finished with his dungeon, the Great Deku Tree dies. In the original, this was sad, but visually it was hard to convey anything meaningful was really happening here, and I’m not even sure I fully clocked how significant things were when I played. In the new Ocarina, there’s no doubt. I found this scene very beautiful, and I think I understand better now why a highly detailed 3D model of the Great Deku Tree was part of the main inspiration for the remake’s look and feel. Go watch this one for yourself, please.

Heading into the meat of the game’s main quest as I reach Hyrule Castle, I’m thinking a lot about what it means for a remake to be “faithful.” By any definition, this Ocarina of Time is a faithful remake. There are slight changes to item positioning and mechanics, but the core remains the same. Even so, my impression thus far is that the Ocarina of Time remake is tonally quite different from the original in a hundred small ways, all of which add up, but not into a single coherent something. I don’t think it’s as simple as saying it’s a lighter game, or more child-friendly, more fleshed out. I can’t sum it up, not yet. And I’m already feeling how reductive it will inevitably be to try and call this better, or worse, or anything more or less than its 28-year-old predecessor. They’re one story, but two totally different experiences, as if made for two different worlds, or even timelinesâthank Hylia, I guess, that that’s the sort of timeline nonsense Link has been messing around with for decades now.

It's an exciting time to be a fan of the MCU, as we're just a month and change away from the next upcoming Marvel movie Avengers: Doomsday hitting theaters. Anticipation is as a fever pitch, especially considering how many beloved characters are included in Doomsday's cast list. That includes Channing Tatum, who is reprising the role of Gambit after appearing in Deadpool & Wolverine (which is streaming with a Disney+ subscription). Tatum recently played that role in a new ad for Dunkin', and his accent seems way more toned down.

Channing Tatum's Gambit accent was pretty wild in Deadpool 3, and there was a running joke about the other characters not being able to understand him. He claimed he wouldn't go "full cajun" for Doomsday, and he did just that in the following Dunkin' ad. In fact, I clocked every single word he said to H.E.R.B.I.E.. Check it out below:

Talk about a game changer. While the Magic Mike icon still looks incredible in the same Gambit costume, Tatum found the right balance with his accent. He's working with the same dialect, but its dialed back so that his dialogue doesn't end up lost in the next Avengers movie. Suddenly I'm even more excited to see him back as the card-throwing mutant in The Russo Brothers' crossover film.

The Avengers: Doomsday trailer briefly showed Gambit fighting Shang-Chi, but this is the first time we're hearing him speak ahead of the movie's release. He's still got the cajun swagger, but now we can actually understand the words coming out of his mouth. I assume we aren't going to get any more jokes about the accent like we did in Deadpool & Wolverine.

Fans who spent years watching the Marvel movies in order were shook when Tatum popped up as Gambit in the third Deadpool movie. He was famously attached to play the role for years, but the project sat in development hell. Originally Disney's acquisition of 20th Century Fox felt like the death knell for him playing the X-Man, but luckily that wasn't the case. I can't wait to see what he brings to the table with Doomsday, especially since his appearance presumably will be way less comedic than the Ryan Reynolds movie.

Not only will Tatum get to play Gambit again in the next Avengers movie, but he'll be appearing alongside the OG stars of the X-Men movies. Namely legends like James Marsden, Ian McKellen, Alan Cumming, Kelsey Grammer, Rebecca Romijn and the late Patrick Stewart.

Avengers: Doomsday will hit theaters on December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. Whether or not Gambit survives the battle against Doctor Doom remains to be seen, but at least we'll be able to understand him this time around.

Two weeks after his uncharacteristically spicy comments on the demise of BioWare, Spector's anger clearly has not subsided.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Two weeks after literally calling "bullshit" on EA's decision to close BioWare, immsim legend Warren Spector has posted a follow-up message on LinkedIn that avoids the spicy language but sounds angrier than ever.

"I recently posted my thoughts about EA’s shuttering of BioWare," Spector wrote. "Those of you who read my post know that I was unhappy. I remain so.

"The tragedy of so many layoffs the last few years hasn’t been lost on me, but for some reason, BioWare hit me on an emotional level nothing before had. I was gut-punched."

But some readers, he continued, replied to say that BioWare's best days were behind it, and that shutting it down was a "sound business decision." Those reactions appear to have re-stoked Spector's rage, as he said those people missed his actual complaint: That the game industry executives who are responsible for these problems are never the ones to suffer the consequences.

"If studio-level people leave, resulting in dilution of talent, someone is creating an environment that pushes them out. Do those culture-killers pay any price?" Spector wrote in his new message. "If executives misread the market, over-hire, or make decisions that result in under-funded, over-funded, poorly-marketed games, do they lose sleep, let alone jobs? Do those same executives suffer like developers when the needs of financial partners and investors take precedence over players, does anyone up there care?

"Is there ANY accountability left in this world?"

Then he took direct aim at Electronic Arts' C-suite with some very large, ugly numbers:

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Those figures represent the total compensation given to EA's executives in its 2026 fiscal year—a single 12-month period. They're also significant increases over the previous year: Wilson, for instance, got $30.5 million in 2025, while Miele's was given $9.1 million.

Ironically, those EA executive salaries aren't even directly related to the BioWare closure. Wilson's $8 million raise (and all the others), which was awarded in part for "meeting all milestones for a high-quality launch of Battlefield 6," came just a few months after laying off employees at the studios that made it—Criterion, Dice, Ripple Effect, and Motive—and entirely shuttering Ridgeline Games, which had been working on a new, more story-focused Battlefield game.

"Tens of thousands of do-ers and makers are out of work and these people think they're worth that kind of compensation?" Spector concluded. "And if you think this is a discussion about 'sound business decisions' I hope you never get anywhere near running a business. Or at least that people have the sense not to go work for you."

Spector's frustration and anger comes through here even more clearly than it did when he dropped his uncharacteristic curse, because it's focused: Waving our hands and bemoaning the bullshit might be briefly cathartic, but pointing the finger at these guys over here and saying "this is why" brings the problem into focus like the sun through a magnifying glass.

Sadly, pushback on compensation packages of this size are extremely rare. An analyst report in 2020, when EA shareholders took the unusual step of rejecting a proposed pay hike for the company's executives, said the failure rate of such proposals was just 2.7% in 2019, and 2.6% in 2018. Wilson was paid more than $21 million that year.

#3757. Parties That Changed the World: Barbie’s Premiere and Gone With the Wind’s Debut

The world’s most famous doll was inspired by a spunky, high-end call girl named Lilli. Described as a “gold digger, exhibitionist, and floozy,” the character of Bild Lilli was created in 1952 by German cartoonist Reinhard Beuthien after he was asked to draw a filler cartoon for the inaugural issue of the tabloid Bild-Zeitung. Lilli, a buxom blonde with a perky ponytail and sky-high stilettos, sat beside a fortune teller. “Can’t you give me the name and address of this tall, handsome, rich man?” she cooed. The cartoon was an instant hit, and in 1955, Lilli was immortalized in plastic.

A year later, Ruth Handler discovered the Lilli doll while on a vacation in Europe. She bought several. One was for her teenage daughter, Barbara, to keep; the rest were brought back to Mattel, the toy company she had cofounded with her husband, Elliot, and businessman Harold Matson. (Mattel is a portmanteau of both men’s names.) Lilli—with comically large breasts, chic outfits, and heavy makeup—was precisely what Handler had been looking for.

Robin Gerber, author of Barbie and Ruth, wrote: “The doll looked too much like a prostitute for the company’s taste,” so Mattel’s design team (slightly) softened Lilli’s exaggerated proportions, renamed her Barbie, after Barbara, and before long, she would become the physical ideal for generations of young girls and women everywhere.

Sixty-four years after Barbie hit shelves, she finally got her close-up in Barbie, a feminist manifesto in a pair of pink stilettos. The film’s premiere and after-party at the Shrine Auditorium marked Warner Bros.’ largest premiere to date—and the cherry on top of a bubble-gum-flavored, years-long marketing blitz. According to Event Marketer, “the affair was like Barbie herself: high-energy, glamorous and very, very, colorful.”

It was a beautiful day in Hollywood. Even by Los Angeles standards, the weather on Sunday, July 9, 2023, was almost impossibly perfect—sunshine, low 70s, and a cool breeze—as if Hollywood itself has been dropped into the fantasy world of Barbie Land.

The event kicked off with a splash. The pink carpet was tricked out with replicas of pieces from the film’s beach scenes: a lifeguard station, a towering lighthouse, faux palm trees, and a 3D ocean wave, with carpeting that shifted colors to mimic sand. A wide range of influencers were invited to get first dibs on photo ops before the stars arrived. But the real showstopper was the two-story replica of Barbie’s Dreamhouse, complete with a 2D faux pool, a DJ spinning tracks, and the trademark spiral slide. “We had to have that slide,” Wendy Robino, SVP of Warner Bros. marketing events, said at the time.

On Sunday, they wore pink: Writer and director Greta Gerwig, along with cast members Issa Rae, America Ferrera, Kate McKinnon, Ryan Gosling, and Michael Cera, turned out for the premiere in every shade of Barbie’s signature color, turning something long dismissed as girly into a celebration of individuality, joy, and girl power.

But the belle of the ball wasn’t one to blend in. After weeks of thinking pink, Margot Robbie—the film’s star and producer—arrived in black. Her custom Schiaparelli look re-created 1960s’ Solo in the Spotlight Barbie: a black sequined dress with a single red rose stitched onto her tulle skirt, matching opera gloves, Manolo Blahnik mules, and a diamond necklace. Movie Star Barbie fully committed to the bit, even clutching a pink handkerchief as she posed in front of a pink Corvette. Robbie’s blond hair was swept into a high ponytail—reminiscent of the one first worn by Lilli.

Following the official screening—marking the first time Barbie was revealed to the public—it was time to party.

The theme was “Barbie’s Blowout Disco Party.” Fittingly, one attraction invited guests inside a glittering, 12-foot pink disco ball. Justin Lefkovitch, whose company Mirrored Media, partnered with Mattel to create it, tells VF the entrance created “a shroud of mystery” for partygoers. Inside, a six-foot 1:1 Dreamhouse showcasing the new Barbie the Movie doll collection was surrounded by gold and silver streamers and over a dozen custom pink disco balls. The goal, Lefkovitch recalls, was to “transport guests into the world of Barbie.”

Nicki Minaj was the first guest to arrive at the party, event producer Austin Johnston tells VF—“five-foot-long hair all the way down to the floor.” A theme park designer by trade, Johnston and his company, AKJohnston, transformed the after-party into what he calls a “pop-up museum.” Barbie Land’s pastel-colored cul-de-sac was re-created as “a 65-foot-tall, 70-foot-wide” inflatable, its landmarks crammed together like a kitschy postcard. At the end of Barbie’s driveway, Mark Ronson presided over a hot pink DJ booth, playing hits from the soundtrack by Ice Spice, Dua Lipa (a.k.a. Mermaid Barbie), and Nicki Minaj—whom Johnston had to “very kindly” ask to get off Barbie’s Corvette.

Tucked beneath the second-floor mezzanine, a series of alcoves became larger-than-life photo sets, with photographers on hand to capture guests in action. Partygoers could retrace Barbie’s journey to the Real World—by bike, boat, and rocket ship—or step inside the Kendom man cave, Weird Barbie’s house, and life-size Barbie and Ken toy boxes. Not everyone hired to re-create Barbie Land had actually seen the movie by then; only a handful were invited to be part of that “really restricted small group,” Johnston says.

At the center of the room, guests sipped pink cocktails under a giant disco ball while an 11-foot, glitter-coated pink B twirled above. Another bar doubled as a fashion show, with four life-size mannequins dolled up for disco in original costumes from the film’s dance number, including Barbie’s gold sequined jumpsuit and the Kens’ matching white-and-gold tracksuits.

Obviously, the food was on theme too. Wolfgang Puck catered the evening’s Barbie-Q, serving grilled salmon, summer melon salad, roasted Pink Fir apple potatoes, char siu glazed grilled chicken, and charred tricolor cauliflower.

Even the night’s corporate sponsors knew better than to steal Barbie’s spotlight. OPI set up a nail salon, and Xbox provided a gaming station where players had their pick of two General Motors rides: Barbie’s Corvette or Ken’s Hummer. A highlight for Johnston was spotting Robbie racing a virtual Hummer while her Australian parents cheered her on. “No one paid her to do that,” he says. “She’s just like, I want to have a drink and play a video game at my premiere.”

For one night in Hollywood, women could be anything. And 84 years earlier, another city had hosted another rager in honor of another larger-than-life heroine. While Los Angeles turned pink for Barbie, Atlanta resurrected the Old South for Scarlett O’Hara.

All hell broke loose when British actor Vivien Leigh was cast as beloved heroine Scarlett O’Hara in the big-screen adaptation of Margaret Mitchell’s epic, Gone With the Wind. Fans and journalists were outraged that such an iconic Southern Belle would be played by a foreigner. At the time, Leigh was yet to star in a Hollywood film and was best known stateside for her affair with Laurence Olivier. Gossip columnist Hedda Hopper sniped: “Out of millions of American women, [producer David O. Selznick] couldn’t find one to suit him.”

Hopper was exaggerating, but not by a lot: During a grueling two-year nationwide search for his leading lady, Selznick reportedly met with over 1,400 actresses. After angry fan letters poured in, Selznick’s publicity machine kicked into overdrive—and eventually, the public came around to the idea that a refined Brit was somehow easier to swallow than a Yankee.

But perhaps the most convincing endorsement came from Leigh’s own leading man. Even Clark Gable, who initially considered Leigh “too demure” for the Southern firecracker, was won over by her dedication and declared she “was Scarlett every minute.” His own casting, meanwhile, had been a dream come true from the thousands who flooded MGM and Selznick’s offices with letters demanding he play Rhett Butler

The shoot was famously plagued by drama, and by the time filming wrapped, the cast and crew had earned themselves a party.

But Selznick had bigger fish to fry—namely, finishing the movie in time for its premiere. He left the party planning to local organizers and his trusted story editor Kay Brown, who had convinced her boss to buy the film rights in the first place. But since Atlanta was still tightly in the grip of Jim Crow, not everyone could join in. Leigh’s costars Hattie McDaniel and Butterfly McQueen were excluded from the festivities.

Selznick argued, unsuccessfully, with local organizers to get McDaniel on the guest list. Gable threatened to not attend the premiere in solidarity with his friend, The Hollywood Reporter stated, but McDaniel ultimately talked him out of it. “While it was unfortunate to exclude Mammy, it was the wisest policy,” Brown wrote, per Matthew Bernstein, former professor of film and media studies at Emory University.

Meanwhile, white Atlanta was gearing up for the party of the century. Former president Jimmy Carter later called it the South’s “biggest event” in his lifetime. According to Time, then governor Eurith D. Rivers was prepared to call in the National Guard, while Mayor Hartsfield urged every woman of Atlanta to dust off her hoop skirts and each man to “sprout a goatee, sideburns, and Kentucky colonel whiskers.”

Hollywood came in hot. Leigh and Gable made their grand entrance by limousine, waving to the 300,000 spectators who lined seven miles of streets in downtown Atlanta—including a number of nonagenarian Confederate veterans who were invited as special guests. Leigh arrived with Olivier while Gable brought his new wife, Carole Lombard. Fun fact: Gable reportedly hadn’t even wanted to play Rhett Butler until Louis B. Mayer offered to help bankroll his divorce so he could marry Lombard.

Of the motorcade, Time wrote: “Crowds larger than the combined armies that fought at Atlanta in July 1864 waved Confederate flags, tossed confetti till it seemed to be snowing, gave three different versions of the Rebel yell, whistled, cheered, goggled.” Leigh wept as the crowd welcomed the British actress “back home,” as if she’d just returned from battle.

The multiday event included a costume ball thrown by the Junior League that would have Abraham Lincoln rolling over in his grave. Decked out in hoop skirts, bustles, and Confederate-era uniforms, 6,000 guests descended on the Municipal Auditorium, which had been transformed into a recreation of the film’s Monster Bazaar. Black participants were relegated to serving or entertaining. Among them was the Ebenezer Baptist Church choir, whose singers reportedly performed dressed as enslaved people in front of a façade of Tara, a fictional plantation from the film. One of the singers was 10-year-old future civil rights hero Martin Luther King Jr.

Vivien Leigh arrived in a velvet gown designed by Walter Plunkett. Though Olivier escorted her costar Olivia de Havilland instead—to keep up appearances—Leigh was the belle of the ball, especially in hometown hero Margaret Mitchell’s absence. Eighteen years earlier, the young novelist had performed a risqué “apache dance” at a charity gala, which cost her her Junior League membership. Now, with Hollywood celebrating her masterpiece, some suspected Mitchell was getting the last laugh by snubbing the biggest party in town.

Young women fangirled all over Gable. According to Time, one woman fainted at the sight of him. Another was given a choice: a Christmas gift or a chance to meet the heartthrob. She chose Gable. After he kissed the 11-year-old, she gasped, “Now am I a woman?”

Governor Rivers declared December 15, 1939, a statewide holiday in honor of Gone With the Wind’s world premiere, the grand finale of the three-day extravaganza. Searchlights swept the Southern sky, and flashbulbs popped as 18,000 spectators crowded Peachtree Street. Even Loew’s Grand Theater got a glow-up. Its Romanesque façade was disguised as a grand Southern plantation—four towering white columns were erected to support a temporary façade with floral garlands, potted trees, and an enormous portrait of Leigh and Gable hung above the entrance.

Inside, all 2,000-plus seats sold out at $10 a pop—the equivalent of about $240 today. That’s not exactly chump change, considering Atlanta was still licking its wounds after the Great Depression. Young women in antebellum costumes greeted guests before Mayor Hartsfield took the stage to kick things off. Selznick and the film’s stars received standing ovations that lasted a full minute. But the loudest cheers were for Mitchell, now in attendance, who joined Leigh and Gable onstage.

The lights dimmed for nearly four hours of melodrama. When Rhett Butler delivered his immortal parting shot—“Frankly, my dear, I don’t give a damn”—the audience reportedly gasped, then erupted in applause as he left Scarlett in his dust.

Before Gone With the Wind—still the highest-grossing film of all time when adjusted for inflation—premieres were usually exclusive screenings in Hollywood or New York. 1939’s antebellum extravaganza turned an entire city into a movie set, setting the stage for modern spectacles like Barbie.

Both parties also offer a revealing snapshot of the societies that threw them. For Gone With the Wind, the industry glorified an imagined past; for Barbie, Hollywood toasted an imagined future. The Barbie premiere wasn’t just a love letter to a feminist film: It was also a giant corporate juggernaut designed to sell a product whose history was tangled up with the very stereotypes the film was questioning. It paid off: Following the film’s theatrical release, Mattel reported a third-quarter increase in worldwide gross billings of 27%, and Barbie toy sales in the United States increased 25% for the July-August combined months compared to the same two-month period a year prior. The immersive premiere, brand collaborations, worldwide activations, and fan participation blurred the line between marketing a movie and creating a cultural event.

The film also became Warner Bros.’ most successful release of all time, grossing $1.4 billion worldwide and making Greta Gerwig the first solo female director admitted into the hallowed halls of the billion-dollar boys club. The premiere celebrated a movie that changed the cultural conversation while handily outgrossing the testosterone-fueled Oppenheimer—a spectacular rebuke to the assumption that chick flicks have a glass ceiling.

Its timing made the celebration particularly potent. In that moment, Hollywood was still finding its footing after the pandemic; the premiere offered something audiences were missing. “It eventized going back to the movies. It eventized the premiere,” says Lefkovitch.

For one night, partygoers got to revel in a fairy tale where women ruled the world. But outside Barbie Land, the irony had all the subtlety of Ken’s Mojo Dojo Casa House. Hollywood was throwing an enormous party celebrating a fantasy of female empowerment while women were still fighting for equality in the real world. There is “definitely some hypocrisy,” agrees Lefkovitch, who made a point of thanking his all-female team.

Decades earlier, Atlanta had thrown its own enormous party, celebrating a fantasy of Southern womanhood while reinforcing the racial and social hierarchies of the real South—and conveniently leaving the horrors of slavery out of the picture. (The film itself did just that, presenting a fictional plantation where the most loyal individuals enjoyed being enslaved.) Black performers were welcome to entertain white audiences, but not to celebrate alongside them; not a single seat inside Loew’s Grand Theater was available to Black moviegoers.

Together, these indignities galvanized the local Black press. In a column for Atlanta Daily World, Reverend John Clarence Wright wrote, “As Atlanta goes mad with the Wind one hundred thousand of her citizens should become more thoughtful than ever of the course that must be pursued to gain their rights as free men and citizens in a land where the spirit of secession and slavery still lives.” With Black moviegoers barred from Southern theaters, the Pittsburgh Courier dryly observed, “Negro reaction… will have to wait until the film comes North.”

The premiere and the film’s success helped propel the NAACP to fight not just individual films, but toward a broader campaign to change Hollywood itself. In 1942, NAACP leader Walter White spoke directly to studio heads in an attempt to persuade them to steer away from demeaning Black stereotypes—like the ones onscreen in Gone With the Wind—and to increase the roles available to Black actors in Hollywood.

White’s approach infuriated the very woman whose absence from the Atlanta premiere had helped expose Hollywood’s hypocrisy: Hattie McDaniel. As a Black woman, McDaniel’s choices were limited—“I’d rather play a maid than be one,” she once said. Writing for Vanity Fair, Hadley Hall Meares noted that McDaniel was “incensed” that White had negotiated with the studios on her behalf, and believed she and her fellow Black actors deserved their own seat at the negotiating table.

McDaniel did get a seat at the 1940 Oscars—but it was at a small table at the edge of the room, separated from her Gone With the Wind costars. The ceremony, after all, was held at the Cocoanut Grove nightclub, which had a strict color line. When her name was called, McDaniel gushed: “I sincerely hope I shall always be a credit to my race and to the motion picture industry.”

Meares described McDaniel’s life as “a tightrope walk.” She was expected to satisfy the white executives who controlled her career, the Black audiences who wanted better representation, and her own ambitions as an actress.

Vivien Leigh also made history that night, becoming the first Brit to win the Oscar for best actress. She dedicated her award to Selznick for his “energy, courage, and very great kindness.” After all, he had been partly responsible for convincing an initially outraged public that Leigh was worthy to play their beloved Scarlett O’Hara. Years later, the Academy lavished Barbie with eight nominations, though it snubbed Gerwig for best director and Robbie for best actress. (Frankly, my dear, they didn’t give a damn about the two women who created Barbie Land.) If Hollywood could build an entire universe in which women ruled the world, why was it still so difficult to imagine one outside the movie theater?

Billie Eilish and Finneas O’Connell took home Barbie’s only Oscar, for best original song. Their winning composition poses Barbie’s existential question while echoing the expectations heaped upon Scarlett, Leigh, McDaniel, Robbie, and Gerwig: “What Was I Made For?”

It turns out the inspiration for Barbie—the quintessential American toy—wasn’t even made for little girls. Lilli dolls were sold to grown men in European tobacco shops and adult toy stores, becoming popular gag gifts. “Men… put them on their car dashboard, dangled them from the rearview mirror, or gave them to girlfriends as a suggestive keepsake,” Gerber wrote. Long before Barbie could be anything, she was something for men.

Eighty-four years apart, Hollywood threw two spectacular parties for women who refused to play by the rules. But the rules were still very much in place when the lights came back up.

#3756. Ocarina Of Time Makes One Of Link’s Strongest Attacks Harder To Use, But There’s An Easy Fix

Nintendo Switch 2The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

If you know 3D Legend of Zelda, you probably have mapped out in your head Link’s basic roster of attacks, which have stood mostly unchanged since the original Ocarina of Time. There’s the roll, the sidestep, the usual array of slashes, the spin attack, and the powerful jump attack. It’s a good move, and exactly what it says it is: you jump, then attack, and do double the damage of a normal smash. Thanks, gravity!

In Ocarina of Time, Link cannot jump freely: only when he is running up on a ledge, where he’ll jump automatically to clear the gap. To do his jump attack, then, the devs made it very easy: simply Z-target an enemy, and press A. Everyone loves this move!

In the remake, though, jumping is different. You can jump at any time using the X button, whether there’s a ledge or an enemy or nothing. This means you have to manually cross gaps, which may trip up some longtime fans. But weirder still is the jump attack, which now requires multiple inputs. You have to target an enemy, press forward, jump with X, and attack with Y. Given the short airtime on Link’s jump, this requires a pretty fast maneuver on the buttons that honestly feels counterintuitive. I kinda hate it.

Thankfully, original director and remake producer Eiji Aonuma recognized how bad this felt, and asked the team to make a workaround. It’s not explained to you in the game’s tutorial, but you can find this information in the menu refresher tutorials after you learn the jump attack in Kokiri Forest. For an easier time of it, target an enemy, tilt the stick forward, and just press A. Link will jump and attack. Blammo!

It still feels a little weird, just because the regular attack button is in a different place from usual, but it’s a lot easier to get the hang of than the clonky X + Y combo. Try it out if you’re struggling to handle enemies!

#3755. One Chicago Stars Who Have Confirmed They Would — Or Wouldn't — Return

The One Chicago universe has become a revolving door of actors — and fans are still hopeful some of the past characters will make a comeback.

Dick Wolf started the Chicago-based family of shows with Chicago Fire in 2012. Two years later, Chicago P.D. gave fans an inside look at how police work in the Windy City. Chicago Med joined the group in 2015.

After more than a decade on air, each show has lost significant actors such as Jesse Spencer, Monica Raymund and and Joe Miñoso on Chicago Fire, Jesse Lee Soffer, Sophia Bush and and LaRoyce Hawkins on Chicago P.D. and Brian Tee and Nick Gehlfuss on Chicago Med. Luckily, a few of the stars are ready and willing to reprise their roles.

Scroll down to see which One Chicago stars have confirmed whether they want to return — or have no plans to come back — to the universe:

As A Big Brother Fan, I’m Living For The A+ Costume Rick Devens’ Wife Used To Celebrate His Win

I’m completely OK with admitting I only started watching Big Brother during Season 28. I’m a Survivor fan, and I jumped on the Big Brother bandwagon about two episodes in after I found out that my guy Rick Devens and my girl Dee Valladares were on the show. Turns out I’m not the only one. On average, Big Brother was up 8% this season over last year, and I’d be willing to bet a bunch of those newbies were Survivor fans. That didn’t stop the hate from the Big Brother core, however.

As a first season viewer, I had a very limited understanding of how this game has been played in the past, and how winners usually land the ultimate prize money. I had seen a few episodes before just from my TV work and knew the gist, but had never committed to watching a full season of the great reality competition series, so I was very much surprised by the fan response to the crossover.

From what I generally saw online, Dee and Devens played Big Brother more aggressively than most former players, latching onto and betraying alliances earlier and more frequently, and generally saying and doing whatever they needed to in order to remain in the game for as long as possible.

In short, they were kind of playing a long haul game of Survivor, only on a different series on the 2026 TV schedule. As someone who watches Jeff Probst’s show, this was familiar and exciting for me, but a lot of the regular fanbase hated it. Even some former Big Brother players were vocal about rooting against Devens and Dee. Heck, even host Julie Chen Moonves was anti-Devens for a time (though she seemingly came around).

Many fans and even alum came out of the woodwork to express anger and dismay about the Survivor cast members joining the show. This includes alum Danielle Reyes, who actually went on to join another reality show, The Traitors, after her Big Brother run. She said during the show’s run she was OK with Dee and Devens playing but certainly didn’t want either to win.

We want to see them play the game, but we don’t want them to win because that’s our kingdom.We don’t want them to come into our Big Brother house and win, when we have this inner struggle of what’s the harder show, Big Brother or Survivor? So that’s where I stand in watching these two play this game.

So, a lot of people who have been involved or watched the show for a long time were not excited about the icons getting a shot at the prize money, and even Big Brother alum Angela Murray was lumped into that.

Apparently, the creative team behind the show did not see this response coming, despite the fact Big Brother fans and alum are notoriously vocal and sometimes toxic. (To be fair, I didn't either, as I thought the Icons made the gameplay really exciting.)

Executive producer Allison Grodner actually told EW the response to having on the icons was a “surprise,” and they thought the cross-promotional connectivity between the two shows would be more positive.

That was a surprise for sure. Everyone has their tribe, right? It’s like the UCLA versus USC kind of idea. We’re all under the CBS banner and it’s all part of the same family, but there’s definitely a territorial thing that happens. And I don’t think we realized how important that would be to our alumni.

The discourse this season was particularly interesting because this isn’t the first time a Survivor player went on Big Brother. Cirie Fields also participated a few years ago. She didn’t win, but she also pulled some moves out of the Survivor playbook during her time on the air. Perhaps that’s the difference. Dee and Devens certainly had an advantage playing together, and not being able to be voted out in Week 1.

Fellow executive producer Rich Meehan also said that Big Brother is not going to bring on just any Survivor player who asks. Dee and Devens were selected specifically because the creative team thought they could hang in the game.

When we were thinking of who we wanted to bring on, it was always about who would be a great Big Brother player. So yes, they have their Survivor legacy and they’re amazing Survivor players, but we’re like, ‘Well, who’s actually gonna be good at this game and who has the personality and the ability to endure three months?

And hang they did. In fact, Rick Devens took home the winning prize, as well as $10,000 in curse money and $50,000 for being America’s Favorite House Guest – despite the haters. Just don’t ask him to choose Survivor o Big Brother over one another.
